cells.tense: Right now you are the one tending this, and it is working from your hands.
cells.ask: Show one thing you're growing to someone and say what you've learned about how it works. Let that be enough for today.
cells.core:
You're the one tending this, and you can see it working. Not watching from a distance — your hands are in it, you're learning how it grows by staying close, and you change what you're doing as things change. You add when it needs more, hold back when it needs less, and you don't call that indecision.

What's growing is getting what it needs because you keep paying attention, not because you're pushing it. The care you give has room in it. When something you've tended finishes, you'll know — you'll be able to let it go, because finishing is the point and not a loss. Until then, you keep feeling for what's needed. That's the work, and it's already in your hands.

cells.tense: You are tending what has not grown yet, bracing for a harvest still out of reach.
cells.ask: Pick one thing you're growing and skip touching it for a day. Notice what your hands want to do when you don't adjust it.
cells.core:
You're already at the harvest, and the harvest isn't here. You can see the finished version of what you're growing — how it should look, what it should have become by now — and when it doesn't match, you push harder. The pushing feels like care. It doesn't land that way.

Somewhere ahead is the version where it's all grown and you can finally exhale, and you're living up there instead of down here where the thing is small and slow. That's the bend. When tending and forcing stop feeling different, what you're growing can't tell you what it needs — it just gets handled. There's another way through: let something develop without you running it, and see what your hands do when nobody's telling them.

cells.tense: You stopped tending what was growing, and you are still standing at a door behind you.
cells.ask: Name one thing you once cared for and say out loud what it became. Say it to someone, or just to the room.
cells.core:
There's something you used to tend — you knew how it grew, when to add and when to hold back — and that's not happening now. You can still feel when a thing needs more or less. You're just not putting your hands on anything. You may be standing still and calling it being careful.

The part of you that senses what's needed has gone quiet, so nothing in front of you gets that same attention. Don't force yourself to care again. Finish something you already started, even something small, and let the finishing put some light back in you. Getting to the end of a thing feeds this. Effort doesn't.

cells.tense: You are already the one tending this, and you describe it as something that just happened.
cells.ask: Say 'I grew that' about one thing you usually say grew on its own. One sentence, out loud.
cells.core:
You've been adjusting this the whole time — you feel when to add, when to hold back, when to blend — and you talk about it like it's just how things went. You are steering, and you haven't said so.

What's growing is growing because you keep paying attention, not because conditions were lucky, and you're the only one in the room who hasn't claimed it. It isn't modesty. Somewhere along the way, naming what you do for it started to feel like overreaching. There's something left to finish here — not a project, just a sentence about what you've been looking after — and letting it land where the rest of your effort already landed.
